display_title: A convincing comparison between self-supervised and domain transfer for anomaly detection with novel collapse avoidance methods

content.title: A convincing comparison between self-supervised and domain transfer for anomaly detection with novel collapse avoidance methods
content.review:
This paper proposes a method to combat feature collapse during model adaptation in anomaly detection (AD), while maintaining performance gains. Feature collapse happens during fine-tuning adaptation of a pretrained model when using a compactness loss and results in all samples, even the anomalous ones, being mapped to the same point. Previous approaches include: removing the bias in all network units as was proposed in DeepSVDD [Ruff 2018]; joint optimization (JO) by using some of the data used to train the pre-trained model [Perera 2019]. This paper proposes 2 novel approaches: 1) adaptive sample-based early stopping (SES) based on a set of checkpoint-saved models after different numbers of iterations and an-inference-time selection of the max anomaly score; 2) continual learning by elastic weight consolidation (EWC). These methods are compared to the baselines DeepSVDD and JO and shown to outperform them on several AD tasks. Another study compares self-supervised approaches to the pretrained approach and show the latter to be more performant. Outlier exposure OE can be added to the proposed method, resulting in new SOT performance for several datasets.
 
 PROS:
 
  * The paper shows convincingly that pre-trained models are superior to self-supervised models, even for datasets where the domain is far from the one used for pretraining (e.g. MVTec,DIOR,FMNIST on ImageNet). 
  
  * The paper proposes two techniques for domain adaptation of the pre-trained weights that mitigate the collapse problem. Those techniques are relatively simple and thus should be reproducible without too much difficulty. 
  
  * The results show that adaptation of the pre-trained weights does provide an extra boost in performance.
  
  * The paper also studies which ResNET block need to be adapted for best results. It is shown that on CIFAR10, adapting only blocks 3+4 of the ResNET, result in the best performance.
 

 CONS:
 
  * The paper does not study the computational complexity of the proposed methods. For example, the SES approach requires multiple inferences with several models and thus becomes much more costly. It is also unclear how the training time is affected by the EWC method.
  
  * It is not clear which anomaly scoring function is used in the experiments. It is stated that several scoring function are evaluated: Euclidian distance, Knn, K-means. However, nowhere is it said which one is finally used.
  
  * It is not specified which baseline results are taken from published papers, and which have been obtained by the authors. The numbers for JO, for example, seem to be obtained by the authors as the JO papers did not use the same datasets (CIFAR, etc.). On the other hand the DeepSVDD numbers seem to come from the published paper.
 

 Overall, this paper provides useful findings and novel approaches to weight adaptation in domain transfer for anomaly detection tasks. It is well written and contains a lot of relevant empirical experiments. The novel methods are clearly explained and should be reproducible. SOT is achieved on several AD benchmarks. A clear accept.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the positive review!

To address the reviewer’s questions:

**Computational complexity:** EWC has nearly the same computational complexity as the naive version at training time. Specifically, the extra number of calculations is $O(N_w)$ where $N_w$ is the number of parameters. In CNNs, there are many fewer weights than the total number of calculations (as the same convolutional weights are applied many times across the image) thus the addition in complexity is minimal - similar to weight decay.  The computational complexity of SES is exactly the same as the standard method at training time, but is T times slower at inference time. As the the standard method is faster than real-time, we do not believe the extra computations would be a significant bottleneck for practical implementation.     

**Anomaly Scoring Function:** We used kNN in all PANDA-Unadapted and PANDA-finetuned (early/EWC/SES) experiments except for the specifically mentioned experiments in 4.2.3. Note that we did not use kNN/k-means for PANDA-OE, instead the classifier probability was used there.

**“which baseline results are taken from published papers?”:** In our experiments, we copied the results from the relevant papers if they were reported, otherwise we computed them ourselves. Specifically - the following results were copied from the mentioned papers: 
* DeepSVDD on Cifar10 - Original paper 
* OCSVM on Cifar10/100, FashionMNIST, CatsVsDogs - Golan and Elyaniv ICLR’18
* MHRot/MHRot-OE on Cifar10 - Original paper.
 
We will add these clarifications to paper before the discussion period ends.

We would be very happy to answer any further questions!

content.title: Lack of novelty and insight
content.review: This paper proposed an algorithm for anomaly detection. The core of the approach includes two parts. One is sample-wise early stopping and anther is a new type of loss. Although the experiment on  the proposed algorithm has better performance on some datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR10, the proposed method does not provide insight understanding about where the performance gain come from. Further, the proposed method is rather a practical assemble of variant existing method which improve the result. For these reason, I do not think this paper is ready to publish.

replying_to: Replying to Lack of novelty and insight

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the review. Although it is rather short, we understand that the reviewer’s main concerns are the novelty and analysis. We would like to push back on these claims. Let us specify some of the ideas in this paper that we think are novel, interesting and impactful.

We are the first to propose an effective solution for feature adaptation for one-class classification (OCC). Novel aspects include:
* No other work in OCC (including DeepSVDD and JO) uses features trained on an external dataset while fine tuning just on the target data.
* We are the first to connect continual learning methods (specifically EWC) with OCC.
* SES is novel, outperforms EWC and removes the need for selecting the number of epochs (in the naive early stopping).

Several of our findings are surprising:
* The fact that DeepSVDD performs no better than linear adaptation is very surprising as it is one of the most cited works in deep anomaly detection.
* The fact that a simple baseline of kNN retrieval on pre-trained features outperforms all previous approaches is very surprising.
* Finding that collapse by itself is not an issue (despite the concerns of JO and DeepSVDD) is surprising and deviates from previous common wisdom.

Finally, providing extensive results on a large set of datasets by the set of PANDA methods will advance the field by serving as a high bar for future methods.

**Performance gain:** A significant part of the performance gains comes from using pretrained features, which are a much stronger representation than self supervised features, used by all the prior works (expect JO). The fact that pretrained features provide boosts over random initialization was of course investigated extensively in other contexts (e.g. [1]) - but surprisingly has not been picked up by the anomaly detection community. We investigated in App.A, why pre-trained features do not boost RotNet-based anomaly detection methods. Our main technical contribution is the gain from feature adaptation. We illustrated the reason for the gain in Fig. 2. The initial pretrained features representation often maps anomalous images near normal images, which have similar attributes w.r.t. the pretraining task. Compactifying the features of the normal data, brings the features of the normal samples closer together, while leaving the features of anomalous images outside the dense region containing the normal samples. This allows kNN (or similar) algorithms to better discriminate normal samples from anomalous ones. 

In terms of analysis, we urge the reviewer to take a look at Sec.4.2 and App. A,B where a wealth of analyses and insights were presented. 

Please let us know if you disagree that the ideas and findings are interesting and that some of them are novel. Given this and our beyond state-of-the-art results, what else can we do to convince the reviewer?

content.title: The paper explores some good practice for anomaly detection, but the contribution is marginal.
content.review:
- The paper lacks of a clear definition of normal and anomaly in images. For example, this could be illustrated in the intro or in each dataset separately. Qualitative results could also be helpful examples. Otherwise, it is hard to understand why each proposed method works, and only quantitative results are not enough to understand the proposed method.

- The paper argues that using pre-trained features in anomaly detection has the combating collapse, but why this happens in anomaly detection or why this problem is especially for anomaly detection is only explained in a few sentences. Another way to ask the question is that is it possible for the proposed method also works for other computer vision tasks or very related task (such as video anomaly detection)? Why?

- The performance of the proposed method achieved good results on five benchmarks, however, it technical contribution is not significant. The contribution mentioned in the paper are more about providing some good practice and analysis about adapting pertained features for image anomaly detection, and its generalization ability is also not clear.

Overall, I would lean to rating 5 before the rebuttal.

replying_to: Replying to The paper explores some good practice for anomaly detection, but the contribution is marginal.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the review and for suggesting that your score may be influenced by the rebuttal. We would like to take advantage of the interactive discussion allowed by ICLR to try to convince the reviewer to modify the score to that of R1.

**Significance:** We tackle one-class classification (OCC) . This is an important setting in machine learning, the main application is indeed anomaly detection. We would like to stress that anomaly detection is a very important and popular field of research with well-cited recent papers published in top ML conferences (e.g. [1-4]). We believe that our results would generalize to video, text and audio anomaly detection for which strong pre-trained feature extractors are easily available. Our scope does have some limitations e.g. our method might be less appropriate for tabular anomaly detection as strong pre-trained feature extractors are not available. We conducted our experiments for the image anomaly detection setting as it is the modality used for evaluation by the most impactful previous papers.

**Collapse:** Feature collapse is a special phenomenon of one-class classification - it does not happen in the multi-class setting and therefore requires special attention. When labels for more than one class exist, the representation does not collapse to a trivial representation. To optimize the loss in multi-class settings, the representation must allow discrimination between classes. Other OCC papers have only been able to tackle it by relaxing the setting. We have been able to do so by embracing asymptotic possibility of collapse but fighting catastrophic collapse (which deteriorates the OCC capabilities of the used features) - please note that collapse still happens if we train indefinitely! Most of the paper is devoted to investigating how to combat mathematical possibility of catastrophic collapse.

We would like to highlight some ideas in this paper that we think are novel and impactful, and are some of our major contributions:

We are the *first to propose an effective solution for feature adaptation for one-class classification (OCC).* Embracing the collapse as a possible mathematical solution allowed us both to use strong pretrained features, trained on an external dataset, and achieve the first beyond-linear adaptation of them for OCC. The lengths undergone by previous methods to avoid the mathematical possibility of collapse, e.g. architectural changes (DeepSVDD) or additional supervision during adaptation (JO) shows *this finding is surprising and goes against the common hypotheses made in the field* (including our own hypothesis when we started this research). 

Moreover, we propose SES which is novel, outperforms EWC and removes the need for selecting the number of epochs (as in the naive early stopping). We are the first to connect continual learning methods (e.g. EWC) and OCC. The findings that *DeepSVDD achieves similar performance to linear whitening* is very surprising (given its popularity), We would also like to note that the *simple baseline of kNN retrieval on pre-trained features outperforms all previous approaches* is very surprising, given other published works in the field. We believe that it will set a much higher bar, and a more promising direction for future methods.

**Illustration of anomalies:** in our paper (in line with nearly all recent image anomaly papers), the normal data are taken to be a single class of a dataset while all other classes are labelled anomalous. For example: in Cifar10, cats may be labelled as anomalous while all other classes such as horses, cars or ships would be labelled anomalous (experiments are performed for all choices of normal class). The only exception is MVTech where the anomalies are abnormalities in an object e.g. for pill, the normal class consists of images of standard pills while an example of an anomaly would be a scratched pill. We repeat that our setting is standard. We will include visual examples in the appendix before the end of the discussion period.

We would like to address all of the reviewer’s concerns. If there are more concerns or that we have insufficiently addressed the current ones, please let us know.

[1] Schlegl, Thomas, et al. "Unsupervised anomaly detection with generative adversarial networks to guide marker discovery." ICIPMI’17 - >700 citations
[2] Ruff, Lukas, et al. "Deep one-class classification." ICML’18 >250 citations
[3] Zong, Bo, et al. "Deep autoencoding gaussian mixture model for unsupervised anomaly detection." ICLR’18  >250 citations
[4] Hendrycks, Dan et al. "Deep Anomaly Detection with Outlier Exposure." ICLR’18  >200 citations

display_title: An OK study on pre-trained model adaptation for image anomaly detection with little conceptual novelty.

content.title: An OK study on pre-trained model adaptation for image anomaly detection with little conceptual novelty.
content.review:
Methodology:
The paper studies the problem of pre-trained model adaptation for image anomaly detection. It is argued that previous model adaptation schemes either lost model capacity (DeepSVDD) or required extra data with marginal improvement (joint optimization). To alleviate these issues, the paper proposes to regularize the model adaptation process by either 1) sample-wise early stopping, or 2) regularize the model deviation from the initial one. For sample-wise stopping, a sequence of adapted models are recorded at fixed intervals during the adaptation process to produce anomaly scores for each query example, and each score is further normalized with those of the normal examples in the training set using the same model. The final anomaly score is the maximum of these normalized scores of the query example. For model deviation regularization, an extra term is added to the original compactness loss to quantify the deviation in the model natural gradient space. Results on several image anomaly benchmarks show that the proposed method improved on both self-supervised and naive model adaptation methods.
            
Pros:
The paper approaches the problem of catastrophic collapse for image anomaly detection from a reasonable perspective, and the proposed solutions are shown to achieve desired effects.  

Cons:
- The overall strategy and most observations are mostly known from other similar applications. 
Early stopping is one of the basic tricks for deep model fine-tuning, and the use of natural gradient for model deviation (elastic weight consolidation (EWC)) was proposed in (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). And all the rest are off-the-shelf implementations for image anomaly detection. Major observations are also not surprising: “We can therefore conclude that ImageNet-pretrained features typically have significant advantages over self-supervised features.” “This shows that one of the main concerns of using pre-trained features, namely, generalizing to distant domains is not an issue in practice.” These are all well known results in many other image modeling applications, and I have a hard time finding much novelty in these aspects.

- Interesting cases are not tested enough to justify the advantages of the proposed methods. 
The proposed sample-wise early stopping (and EWC too) compares only slightly favorably to the naive one that stops after a fixed number of iterations (fig 4). What about some other baseline adaptive early stopping schemes? E.g., cross-validating the #fine tuning iteration on the validation set, and so forth. I doubt that these easier early stopping methods would work better at a far less cost of the proposed SES as the latter needs to do T times number of inference for a single example. If so, why bother using the more expensive SES? 

Minor comments:
It looks to me that there are typos in some critical parts of the paper.
- eq (3), it should be L(x, y; \theta), instead of L(x,y); \theta, right? The latter does not make sense to me…
- eq (5), it should be log(1-\sigma(w\phi(x))) instead of log(\sigma(1-w\phi(x))), right?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the review. We would like to push back on the two concerns of the reviewer with the hope that further explanation would prompt and increase to the score of R1.

Our method achieved the **best results by far in image anomaly detection on an extensive number of benchmarks**. Let us emphasize the most interesting and/or impactful messages of this paper:

**Novelty:** Using features pre-trained on an external dataset and finetuning on the target data (while not having to retain the original images) has not been suggested by any other OCC paper  (including DeepSVDD and JO). Adapting networks under the OCC setting requires the introduction of new methods to anomaly detection - EWC and SES. While EWC was indeed proposed by Kirkpatric et al. (and we cite and build on this prior work), continual learning methods were not used for OCC. We do not claim novelty for EWC, of course, but rather for identifying that it can mitigate catastrophic forgetting in OCC feature adaptation. We comment on SES (being another novelty) in detail below.

**Surprising findings:**  The fact that DeepSVDD *performs no better than linear adaptation* is very surprising as it is one of the most cited works in deep anomaly detection. Its limited performance results from its aim to limit the expressivity of the networks. Other prior works included more data during training (JO) in order to avoid collapse, which limits their performance. We find that the *asymptotic possibility of collapse by itself is not an issue*, a surprising result that deviates from previous common wisdom. Finally, we found the fact that a *simple kNN baseline outperforms all previous methods* very surprising.

**Impact on the field:** Providing extensive results on a large set of datasets by the PANDA methods, that achieve much better performance than current methods, will advance the field by serving as a high bar for future methods.

**Advanced adaptation methods:** We would like to emphasize that the objective of the new adaptation methods is not to outperform early stopping but rather to remove the dependence on the ad-hoc number of iterations and replace it by a more principled method. We presented two new ways of doing it: 
**EWC:** Utilizing EWC, which we show for the first time to be effective for OCC (Kirkpatric et al. used it for multi-class problems), is able to mitigate catastrophic forgetting - while not specifically trying to prevent the possibility the features will asymptotically collapse. 
**SES:** This is actually quite a subtle idea. As mentioned before, OCC is different from the typical supervised-classification scenario that feature adaptation methods were applied on. In particular, the validation set contains no anomalies and cannot be used to validate the gap between normal and anomalous data for a particular model. PANDA does not overfit in the usual sense i.e. there is nearly no gap between train and validation compactness scores on normal data - the score ratio between train and test for all epochs will be close to 1 (this is shown the lower line in Fig. 1 which is roughly constant). SES strives to select a model for which the normal-anomaly score gap is large in an unsupervised way. SES does so by estimating the normal-anomalous gap on the single example seen at test time and is therefore able to select a good stopping epoch. In the case where a validation set of anomalous data is available, the idea proposed by the reviewer will be effective, but please remember that in the standard setting used by most papers (including ours) this data is unavailable.

We thank the reviewer for suggesting editorial improvement. They will be added to the manuscript before the end of the discussion period.

If the reviewer still believes this is not sufficiently interesting, we would really appreciate clarifying the reasons so we could address them. We would be very happy to clarify any further points or provide further evidence.
